lesson.title: Knowing When It Pays Off: Deciding Whether to Stratify
lesson.summary: Stratifying only helps when the strata are internally homogeneous but differ meaningfully from each other on the variable being measured; when that condition fails, stratified sampling adds complexity without adding precision.
lesson.body:
Stratified random sampling is not automatically better than a simple random sample, and part of designing a good study is recognizing when the extra effort of forming strata is actually worth it. The key condition is this: stratification helps precision when individuals within each stratum are relatively similar to one another on the variable being measured, while the strata themselves differ meaningfully from each other on that same variable. When both of those conditions hold, splitting the population into strata removes a real source of variability from the sampling process. When they do not hold, stratifying adds logistical complexity without buying any real statistical benefit.

Return to the high school cafeteria example to see why the condition matters so much. Stratifying by grade level was worthwhile only because there was good reason to think opinions about cafeteria food actually differ by grade, perhaps due to different lunch privileges or different times students eat. Now imagine a different variable entirely: suppose the school instead wants to know what fraction of students bring a phone to school, and virtually every student across all four grades carries a phone. In that case, grade level is not meaningfully related to the variable of interest, phone ownership is roughly uniform across freshmen through seniors, so stratifying by grade would not reduce variability in the estimate at all compared to just taking a plain SRS of 90 students; it would only add the extra work of organizing the population into grade level lists first.

A useful mental test is to ask whether the variable used to define the strata is a plausible lurking variable connected to the outcome being measured, echoing the same kind of thinking used earlier when identifying confounding. If splitting the population along some characteristic, grade level, geographic region, gender, income bracket, would plausibly separate people into groups with noticeably different average responses, that characteristic is a strong candidate for stratification. If the characteristic has little to do with how people would answer, it is not a useful stratifying variable, even if it happens to be an easy, convenient way to divide up a list of names.

There is also a cost side to the decision that goes beyond statistical precision. Forming strata requires the researcher to already know, in advance, which subgroup every individual in the population belongs to, information that is not always available or easy to obtain. A national survey can reasonably stratify by state, since that information exists in advance for essentially every resident, but stratifying by a subtler trait like political engagement level would first require measuring that trait for the entire population, which may be just as hard as the original survey it was meant to improve.

The overall guideline students should take away is this: stratify when there is a strong, defensible reason to believe the stratifying variable is tied to the response, since only then does grouping like with like actually shrink the variability that a margin of error has to account for; otherwise, a well executed simple random sample, without the added complexity of strata, remains a perfectly sound and often more practical choice.
